short: Under GLBA a lender stays responsible for customer data it gives an AI vendor. The Safeguards Rule requires vendor selection, contract safeguards and ongoing assessment, and the Privacy Rule limits the vendor to the purpose the data was shared for.
title: AI Vendor Due Diligence Under GLBA
subtitle: What the Safeguards Rule and the Privacy Rule require before a lender shares customer data with an AI vendor
body_html:
A lender that hands customer data to an AI vendor is still the party the Gramm Leach Bliley Act holds responsible for it. The Safeguards Rule requires you to choose vendors that can protect the data, bind them by contract, and keep checking them. The Privacy Rule limits what the vendor may do with the data once it has it. This page sets out what each rule says and what that means when the vendor is an AI company.

Which rule applies to you

GLBA is enforced by different agencies for different institutions. Nonbank financial institutions under Federal Trade Commission jurisdiction, which includes mortgage lenders, mortgage brokers and finance companies, follow the FTC Safeguards Rule at 16 CFR Part 314. Banks follow the Interagency Guidelines Establishing Information Security Standards issued by their prudential regulator, and they also answer to the 2023 Interagency Guidance on Third Party Relationships. Both tracks reach the same place on vendors: due diligence before you sign, a contract that requires safeguards, and monitoring afterward.

What the Safeguards Rule requires for a vendor

The rule defines a service provider as anyone that receives, maintains, processes or is otherwise permitted access to customer information by providing services directly to you. An AI vendor that receives loan files, transcripts or account data to do a job for you fits that definition. Section 314.4(f) then sets three duties. You must take reasonable steps to select and retain providers capable of maintaining appropriate safeguards, require those safeguards by contract, and periodically assess each provider based on the risk it presents.

Those duties sit inside a wider program. The rule also requires a written risk assessment, encryption of customer information in transit and at rest, multi factor authentication, and a qualified individual who reports to your board. An AI tool that touches customer information belongs in that risk assessment like any other system.

What the Privacy Rule lets the vendor do with the data

Under Regulation P, 12 CFR Part 1016, sharing nonpublic personal information with a nonaffiliated third party normally requires a privacy notice and a chance for the consumer to opt out. Vendors are usually covered by an exception. Section 1016.13 allows sharing with a service provider that performs services for you, on the condition that your contract prohibits the provider from disclosing or using the information other than to carry out the purposes for which you disclosed it. Section 1016.14 covers processing and servicing a transaction the consumer asked for, and section 1016.11 limits reuse and redisclosure by whoever receives the data.

This is where AI contracts need care. Our reading is that a clause letting the vendor train its general models on your customer data is a use beyond the purpose you shared it for, and it is hard to square with the service provider exception. Ask for a written commitment that your data is not used for training, and check that the commitment covers the vendor's subcontractors.

Sharing de identified data with an AI vendor

Regulation P says personally identifiable financial information does not include information that does not identify a consumer, such as aggregate information or blind data without personal identifiers like account numbers, names or addresses. That is section 1016.3(q)(2)(ii)(B). So data that truly identifies no one falls outside the Privacy Rule. The risk is in the word truly.

A mortgage file is unusually easy to re identify. The property address, the loan amount and the recording date appear in public county land records, so a file stripped of the borrower's name can still point to one household. If a vendor could reasonably link the records back to people, you have shared nonpublic personal information and every duty above applies. Treat a pilot or evaluation on de identified data as a vendor relationship anyway: sign the contract, prohibit re identification, and limit the fields to what the test needs.

When the vendor has an incident

Since May 13, 2024 the Safeguards Rule has required a covered institution to notify the FTC as soon as possible, and no later than 30 days after discovery, of a notification event involving the unencrypted information of at least 500 consumers. An incident at a vendor holding your customer information can start that clock. Your contract should require the vendor to tell you promptly, give you the facts you need to count affected consumers, and cooperate with your notice.

Questions to put to an AI vendor

These are practical questions that follow from the rules above. They are our checklist, not regulatory text.

  • Where is our data stored and processed, and by which subcontractors?
  • Is any of our data used to train or improve models, yours or anyone else's?
  • How long is data kept, including prompts, outputs and logs, and how is deletion proven?
  • Is data encrypted in transit and at rest, and who at the vendor can read it?
  • How fast will you notify us of an incident, and what will the notice contain?
  • What independent assurance can we see, such as a SOC 2 report, and may we audit?
  • What happens to our data when the contract ends?

Staff using public AI tools

The quickest way to break these rules is an employee pasting a customer's details into a consumer chatbot. That is a disclosure of nonpublic personal information to a third party with no contract in place. Give staff an approved tool under business terms that rule out training on your data, block the consumer versions on work devices where you can, and say so in a written policy.
